 Quantitative Analysis of Urban Location Characteristics, Environmental Im-
pacts, and Policy Strategy Effects on Mega Sporting Events 
Sport mega-events create substantial social and economic value but also impose significant envi-
ronmental costs. Therefore, it is of great importance to understand the environmental impacts of these 
events and to explore how changes in their planning may alter these impacts. 
Firstly, taking Super Bowl LIX in New Orleans as the baseline, 17 quantitative indicators covering 
both environmental impacts and city location characteristics are established. Reasonable value ranges 
and physical interpretations specified based on published literature and statistical data. In addition, 8 
sub-criteria are introduced to capture sustainability factors relevant to multi-sport competition.  
Secondly, the relationship between city location characteristics and environmental impacts is 
quantitatively characterized. City features are first reduced by principal component analysis (PCA) 
based on Pearson correlations, and a multiple linear regression model is then constructed with the 
principal component scores as explanatory variables, yielding a PCA-based urban environmental 
impact model. Three latent dimensions—infrastructure level (PC1), climate–geographical conditions 
(PC2), and population density (PC3)—jointly explain about 85% of the total variance. Grid carbon 
intensity, renewable energy share, public transit coverage, and the share of green or low-carbon travel 
are identified as the main structural drivers of environmental performance. 
Thirdly, an environmental impact evaluation model is developed within this multi-indicator 
framework. ARIMA models are applied to forecast future city characteristics for U.S. cities that have 
already hosted the Super Bowl and to project 2029 features for three NFL cities that have not yet 
hosted—Charlotte, Buffalo, and Kansas City. The forecasted features are then input into the principal 
component regression model to obtain future environmental indicators, which are further aggregated 
into composite scores using the entropy-weight method. The results indicate that Santa Clara ex-
hibits the best environmental performance among historical hosts, while Kansas City attains the high-
est score among the three potential new hosts. 
Fourthly, the model is extended to comprehensive mega-events such as the Summer Olympic 
Games. Building on the single-event evaluation framework, additional indicators reflecting the sus-
tainability of multi-venue, multi-sport events are introduced, and a composite venue evaluation 
model based on principal component regression is developed . The results show that for single 
events, environmental pressure is concentrated mainly in short-term peaks in water use and spectator 
transport emissions, whereas for multi-venue, multi-sport events,  long-term effects  from Olympic 
Village energy consumption, venue network layout, and post-event venue reuse play a more dominant 
role. After applying the entropy-weight method to derive composite environmental scores, Los Ange-
les emerges as the best-performing host under the comprehensive event scenario.  
Finally, a sensitivity analysis is conducted to quantify the influence of key policy variables on 
environmental impacts. The infrastructure investment, energy procurement, and transport-mode shifts 
are abstracted as three policy control variables and mapped, via interpretable transfer functions, 
to changes in city characteristics and environmental indicators. The resulting effects are then evaluated 
using an environmental composite score within the broader assessment model, confirming the robust-
ness of the approach.

Research on Comprehensive Environmental Assessment of Sport
Mega-Events
As public awareness of sustainability grows, mega sporting events are facing stricter scrutiny and public
pressure. Beyond excitement and huge economic gains, comprehensive evaluations for such events are in urgent
need in order to strive for greener, more responsible decision making. This is especially obvious when it comes
to the case study of Super Bowl LIX in New Orleans. Even though the NFL had taken measures to mitigate the
environmental footprint, Super Bowl LIX still left a significant impact on the local environment.
In this study, we primarily developed two sets of comprehensive evaluation metrics for the Super Bowl and the
World Cup, respectively.
Covering more than 14 contributing factors, our City Impact Evaluation Model (CIEM), which evaluates
potential host cities for Super Bowl, is established based on 5 core indices of environmental impact: Carbon Emis-
sion Index (CEI), Energy Consumption Index (ECI), Water Consumption Index (WCI), Air Quality Index (AQI),
and Landfill Index (LFI). Next, we determined the weights of each index during multi-criteria decision-making
(MCDM) by strategically combining the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) and the Entropy Weight Method
(EWM). The AHP-EWM MCDM provides an adaptable, transparent, and structured framework for weighting,
ensuring objectivity within subjectivity while yielding a set of balanced, practical results. Finally, we utilized
Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) to generate a comprehensive scoring for
each potential host, recommending Inglewood, California, for future Super Bowl events, which has the highest
scoring.
To adapt CIEM to assess the eligibility of potential host countries for the World Cup, we established our
National Impact Evaluation Model (NIEM) . NIEM encompasses 6 core indices of environmental impact: CEI
(adapted), ECI (adapted), WCI (adapted), AQI (adapted), LFI (adapted), and a new Environmental-Industrial Index
(EII). Similarly, NIEM employs a smart combination of both AHP and Criteria Importance Through Intercriteria
Correlation (CRITIC) due to the interdependence between the 6 indices; the AHP-CRITIC MCDM guarantees
transparency and objectivity within subjectivity and effectively handles the interconnections of the data. Ulti-
mately, TOPSIS is again used to yield a composite score for each potential host country, selecting Germany with
the highest score as the best choice for hosting future World Cup events.
Notably, we conductedsensitivity analyses for CIEM by adjusting the AHP-to-EWM ratios and the numbers
of participants in a Super Bowl event. First, AHP-to-EWM ratios determine which weighting method is more
influential. By slightly fluctuating the ratio, our final scoring for the potential host cities remained approximately
unchanged, proving CIEM to be robust and reliable. Second, the number of participants is also altered, resulting
again in slight fluctuation in the results, further corroborating CIEM’s robustness and reliability.
Assessing CIEM and NIEM, both integrate a relatively wide range of contributing factors that constitute
5 and 6 indices, respectively, ensuring comprehensiveness. Moreover, both models are adaptable to a variety
of host cities or countries. CIEM can be applied to most US states, while NIEM can be used to evaluate most
countries across the world. Nonetheless, due to the lack of data, CIEM and NIEM are both approximation models
based on assumptions. If enhanced with data currently unavailable, CIEM and NIEM will be considerably more
accurate and practical.

Our job recommendation model takes into consideration nine job features: Net Weekly Wage, 
Flexibility, Hours, Location, Work Environment/Culture, Social Interaction, Physical Activity, Interest and 
Prerequisites. The first step of our model is to eliminate jobs based on prerequisites and the student’ 
experience. We did so using a Decision Tree to filter out all preferentially invalid jobs. Then, we modified

for the job feature inputs were calculated and normalized using a Box-Cox Transformation and Min-Max 
Normalization when necessary. The Analytic Hierarchy Process created a weighted sum of these indices 
based on the student’s preferences. Last, we performed a Cost-Benefit Analysis to create final job indices 
which we quantitatively sorted by magnitude to rank our job recommendations. 
 We applied our model in two applications: one to recommend job categories and another to 
recommend a specific job. Both applications follow similar processes except for different job features and 
indices calculation. The applications produced job recommendation results for ten fictional persons that 
were then compared with a simpler tiebreaker ranking method. It became clear that our model was far 
superior because it was able to account for absolute preferences rather than relative preferences. 
Furthermore, because our model implemented a weighted sum, it also took into account trade-offs between

Our final goal is to develop algorithms for ranking roller-coasters that can be employed in

who just needs an objective ranking, and the professional who wants a personalized ranking

To correct for missing data, we designed Linear Iterative Imputation, a technique that uses 
linear regression to iteratively impute the features based on which useful features (statistically 
significant at 5%) are selected by the linear model to impute the value of the missing one. In our 
problem, we first imputed speed, as the variable in the constructed linear model, height, was 
present in all entries where speed is missing. Then we imputed length with the variables duration 
and speed, as now all the entries with missing length had duration and speed. We then repeat this 
to create 6 linear models that imputes the 6 variables in which there are missing values. Majority 
of our models achieve over R2 of 0.5, which exceeds greatly the R2 of 0 from mean imputation. 
After imputing the dataset, we grouped the descriptors of the rollercoaster into 3 groups:

variables normalized and the weights chosen to balance the importance of each variable group. 
We further corrected differences in construction methods to ensure fair comparisons. 
The second one, called the Personalized Rollercoaster Ranking (PRR), employs the Analytic 
Hierarchy Process (AHP). As roller-coaster ranking is indeed a very subjective process, we ask 
the user to enter his/her own preference of the 3 variable groups. Then using AHP we can devise 
personalized regression weights to use in GRR in order to achieve a final ranking.

account the casual and the enthusiast. In the first case, our baseline algorithm confirms the
